sources.title: NYC Parks Trails (five boroughs)
sources.url_comment: THE PORTAL PAGE A REVIEWER READS, not the address the fetcher uses - that is `domain` plus `dataset_id`, assembled by lib/socrata.py's dataset_url(). Recorded this way round because every other entry's `url` is something a person can open and see the data behind, and a bare SODA resource endpoint is not; nothing in the pipeline reads `url` for a source of this kind.
sources.steward: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below. NYC's terms are STATED and statutory - Local Law 11 of 2012 (Admin Code 23-502(d)) makes the city's published data sets available without registration requirement, license requirement, or usage restrictions - which makes this the first entry in the registry that needs neither an ask nor an authorisation to stand on. The maintainer's authorisation of 2026-09-15 is recorded alongside it for the attribution rider that block describes, not for the right to use the data.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.foot_comment: NO FOOT FILTER, BECAUSE THERE IS NO USE COLUMN TO FILTER ON, and that is a widening of export_nearby_trails.py's keep-everything default worth stating rather than inheriting. That default is grounded in the sentence 'a source with no use flags at all keeps every row, because NYNJTC and Mohonk publish hiking trails and nothing else' - and NYC Parks is NOT that: measured live 2026-09-15, 198 rows are bridle-named and 2,174 of 7,059 are `Class V : Fully Developed`, which is a paved park path rather than a trail. The layer publishes no FOOT/BIKE/HORSE matrix of any kind, so there is nothing to allowlist; what it publishes instead is `class` and `surface`, which describe how developed a path is and not who may use it. Everything here is walkable on foot - a paved park path and a bridle path both are - so keeping every row is right, and it is right for a different reason than the default's. The maintainer's 2026-08-18 decision ('It's OurHike, not OurBike') bites on per-use flags and finds none here. What would settle it properly is NYC Parks publishing a use column, which they do not.
sources.blaze_comment: REGISTERED AS THE NEUTRAL, AND THE COLOUR IS NOT LOST SO MUCH AS NEVER DECLARED. This layer has no blaze field. What it has is `trailmarkersinstalled`, a plain Yes/No - 4,017 against 3,042, measured live 2026-09-15 - which says WHETHER a marker is nailed to the trees and never which colour it is. The colour is instead inside the NAME: `trail_name` reads 'Blue Trail' 549 times, 'Orange Trail' 326, 'White Trail' 251, 'Red Trail' 215, 'Yellow Trail' 153. Parsing a blaze out of those strings would be easy and is deliberately NOT done here, for the reason nynjtc_highlands_trail registers its absent blaze as the neutral rather than as the teal the trail wears on the ground: a colour this project inferred from a name is this project's claim, not NYC Parks', and a hiker matching a painted blaze against a drawn one cannot tell which of those they are looking at. The honest version of that inference, if it is ever wanted, is a reference/blaze_mapping.json table keyed on the exact name strings and reviewed row by row - the shape the other sources' tables already have - and not a regular expression in an exporter. @unvalidated either way: nobody has checked a single one of those 1,494 colour-named segments against a marker in the field.
sources.name_comment: HALF THIS LAYER HAS NO NAME, and it is worth knowing before a screen tries to print one. Measured live 2026-09-15 across 7,059 rows: 'Unnamed Official Trail' 3,448, 'Name TBD' 239, 'TBD' 88 - 3,775 rows, 53%, whose name field carries a placeholder rather than a name. `park_name` is populated on every row and is the useful label for those (Pelham Bay Park, Van Cortlandt Park, Prospect Park), which is a display decision for features/NEARBY_TRAILS.md rather than a registry one. ACTED ON rather than merely recorded, which is what this comment said and did not do when it was first written: `name_placeholders` below makes export_nearby_trails.py read these three values as an ABSENT name. Without it, measured on the live layer, 'Unnamed Official Trail' totals 128.7 miles - past NAMED_TRAIL_THRESHOLD_MILES - so it shipped one overview feature named 'Unnamed Official Trail' with through_route true, drawn at through-route weight across five boroughs beside the Appalachian Trail and labelled that on the map.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1432, from the maintainer's own ask (2026-09-15: 'I live in NYC and will be able to test the app easiest here'). NYC_SOURCE_SURVEY.md surveyed everything within a day of the city and had no row for the city itself; reference/nynjtc_hike_routes.json already carried the hole as a held hike - 'Van Cortlandt Park, NYC Parks: only one Old Croton Aqueduct edge within 2.5 km; no source registered for NYC Parks'. Found by searching the NYC Open Data catalogue API (api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1) rather than by guessing a URL. Registered by hand: discover_sources.py walks ATC's Experience Builder app, and this is not an ArcGIS layer at all.
sources.notes: 7,059 line segments across 73 parks, every figure in this note measured live against the portal 2026-09-15. BY PARK, the twelve largest: Pelham Bay 766, Van Cortlandt 663, Alley Pond 516, Prospect 376, Central Park 312, Forest Park 268, Inwood Hill 252, Wolfe's Pond 251, Cunningham 242, Marine Park 218, Clove Lakes 213, LaTourette 168. Fields park_name/trail_name/class/surface/difficulty/width_ft/gen_topog/date_collected/parkid/trailmarkersinstalled; geometry is MultiLineString in WGS84, and the whole layer returns in a single request (7,059 features, 5.2 MB) so lib/socrata.py's paging loop is not exercised by it today. THE DATASET DESCRIPTION UNDERSTATES ITS OWN SCOPE, which is the survey's rule 3 in miniature and the reason the count above was read from the data rather than the page: the description says 'paths or trails in designated Forever Wild areas of NYC Parks', but Central Park and Prospect Park are neither Forever Wild nor absent - they are the fourth and fifth largest parks in the layer. AND THAT SENTENCE WAS READ AS A COVERAGE CLAIM WHEN IT IS A COUNT, which is the correction #1530 makes and the reason the rest of this paragraph exists. Measured 2026-09-16 by spike_central_park_paths.py, clipping this layer to NYC Parks' own boundary polygons: Central Park's 312 rows are 6.98 MILES inside an 839-acre park - 37 m per segment, 0.0083 mi/acre - against Prospect Park's 376 rows making 14.32 miles inside 478 acres, 0.0299 mi/acre. A FACTOR OF 3.6 OUT OF ONE LAYER SURVEYED BY ONE STEWARD, which is what makes this a fact about Central Park rather than about the dataset. The independent check says the same thing louder: against the city's planimetric sidewalk polygons (52n9-sdep), 80.7 acres of paved walkway surface inside Central Park and 35.4 inside Prospect, this layer draws 10-17% of Central Park's walkway and 48-80% of Prospect's (the band is an area divided by an assumed 3-5 m width, @unvalidated, and the spike's WALKWAY_WIDTH_BAND_M says what would settle it). SO THE DESCRIPTION WAS CLOSER TO RIGHT THAN THIS NOTE GAVE IT CREDIT FOR: what the layer holds in Central Park is roughly its Forever-Wild-shaped corners - the Ramble, the North Woods, the Hallett sanctuary - plus paved fragments, and not the park's path network. 'Not absent' and 'covered' are different claims and only the first one was ever checked here. `class` is NYC Parks' own five-step development scale (Fully Developed 2,174, Developed/Improved 2,066, Highly Developed 2,028, Simple/Minor 718, Minimal/Undeveloped 73) and `surface` splits Dirt 2,809 / Paved 2,603 / Gravel 582 / Wood Chips 436 / Sand 258 / Boardwalk 125 / Concrete 123, so this is a mixed network of woodland trail and paved park path rather than a backcountry layer, and a hiker's expectation of it should be set accordingly. THE FRESHNESS FIGURE AND THE SURVEY FIGURE ARE DIFFERENT NUMBERS AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON THE GROUND. rowsUpdatedAt read 2026-09-03 and the portal declares a monthly update automation, so the DATASET moves. But `date_collected` is per-segment and spans 2013-10-17 to 2026-08-18, distributed 2013:1,594 2014:2,198 2015:990 2016:143 2017:50 2018:38 2019:39 2020:42 2021:773 2022:206 2023:139 2024:144 2025:644 2026:55, four rows null - so 4,782 of 7,059 segments, 68%, were last surveyed in 2013-2015, and every Central Park row sampled carries a 2014 date. A monthly refresh of a file whose rows are twelve years old is a fact about the file, not about the trail, and CLAUDE.md's 'never let a display outrun its source' is the rule that bears on it: whatever surfaces this must not present a 2026 dataset date as though it were a 2026 survey. No status or closure column exists in this layer, so every kept row exports as open and the export invents nothing.

sources.title: NYC Public Restrooms (operational)
sources.steward: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below - the same statutory grant that covers nyc_parks_trails and nyc_dot_greenways.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.where_comment: OPERATIONAL ONLY, and this is a status filter rather than a scope one (#1461). Measured live 2026-09-15: Operational 975, Not Operational 73, Closed for Construction 17, Closed 1, of 1,066. A privy pin is read as `there is one here`, and drawing a boarded-up one is the same shape of wrong answer as drawing a dry spring - so the 91 that are not operational are excluded at the portal rather than shipped with a caveat the map has no room to print. THE COLUMN IS WHY THIS LAYER SHIPS AT ALL: it is the contrast POI_COVERAGE_SURVEY.md §10 draws against the drinking fountains, whose `featuresta` reads Active on every single row. Real variance is what a status column has to have before it can be believed.
sources.scope_comment: EVERY OPERATOR, which is the maintainer's call of 2026-09-15 over the narrower reading. The survey described this as `multi-agency (DPR, DOT, DCP, DCAS, NYPL, BPL, QPL, MTA)`; the live `operator` column is wider and less tidy than that - NYC Parks 728, NYPL 91, NYC Parks Concessionaire 71, QPL 63, BPL 62, Hudson River Park 11, NYC DOT/JCDecaux 6, Brooklyn Bridge Park 4, LIRR 3, then conservancies and business improvement districts with one or two each. By `location_type`: Park 824, Library 216, Privately Owned Public Space 14, Public Plaza 7, Transit 5. THE ARGUMENT FOR ALL OF THEM is that in a city the nearest toilet is the one that counts and a hiker on the Manhattan waterfront is closer to a library than to a park building; the argument against, recorded because it is real, is that the same pin then means something different here from what it means in the Catskills, where `privy` is a box over a hole that a club digs. What keeps that honest is export_nearby_poi.clip_to_network, which drops any amenity further than NETWORK_BUFFER_FEET from a published line - so a library toilet ships only where somebody walking a trail could actually reach it.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1452, probed alongside the drinking fountains; registered by https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1461.
sources.notes: 975 of 1,066 rows ship after the `where`. The layer carries `changing_stations`, `accessibility`, `hours_of_operation` and `open` besides the status; none of them is exported yet, and `hours_of_operation` is the one most worth having next - a privy that is locked at dusk is a different answer from one that is not.
sources.boundary_source_comment: WHY A BOUNDARY AND NOT A WIDER RING (#1493). `NETWORK_BUFFER_FEET` asks how far this point is from a published trail line, which is the right question on a corridor and the wrong one in a city: in a park the PARK is the destination and the path through it is incidental. Measured 2026-09-15 against the UA release: the 500 ft ring admits 982 of 3,195 fountains and 249 of 975 restrooms, and in Central Park alone 182 of 221 points do not ship - 82% - with the losses falling on the Great Lawn, the Reservoir's outer edge and playgrounds set back from a drive. The ring is kept as an OR rather than replaced: 34 fountains ship today that are NOT inside any park boundary, near a line and outside a property, and a replacement would drop them. Measured the same day, 717 of 975 restrooms sit inside one (73.5%), the boundary genuinely discriminating - it drops the libraries, the privately owned public spaces and the transit entries.

sources.title: NYC Parks Drinking Fountains (outdoor types)
sources.steward: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below - the same statutory grant that covers nyc_parks_trails and nyc_dot_greenways.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.confidence_floor_comment: EVERY ROW, NOT SOME (#1461), and this key exists because there was no way to say it. `featuresta` reads `Active` on ALL 3,849 rows - measured live 2026-09-15, zero variance - so the layer carries nothing about whether any given fountain works. Shipping at the default CONFIDENCE_HIGH would assert of every fountain the thing the source cannot say about a single one, which is the confidently-wrong-prediction FEATURES.md names as more dangerous than an honest unknown, on `out of water`, which is one of CLAUDE.md's four ways this app can hurt somebody. OPRHP's `public_flag_sets_confidence` was the nearest existing mechanism and answers a different question - a per-ROW flag from an org that does distinguish. This is a floor on the LAYER.
sources.where: fountainty in ('A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'Double A', 'E High Low', 'F High Low', 'F High Low and Dog', 'E and Dog', 'F and Dog', 'Bottle Filler', 'Bottle Filler Fountain', 'Bottle Filler High Low', 'Bottle Filler Wall', 'CS Metal', 'CS Concrete', 'CS Metal High Low', 'CS concrete', 'Pedestal', 'Pedestal High Low', 'Pedestal Wall', 'Pedestal High Low and Dog', 'Monument', 'Stone', 'Drinking Fountain Sink Combination')
sources.where_comment: AN ALLOWLIST, NOT A DENYLIST, and the direction is the whole point (#1461): a `fountainty` value NYC Parks adds tomorrow is excluded until somebody looks at it, where a denylist would ship it on the assumption it is drinkable. Measured live 2026-09-15: 3,195 of 3,849 rows kept, 654 excluded, over 39 distinct values. WHAT THE LETTERS ARE, because this filter was impossible to write until it was answered: the dataset's own published Data Dictionary link is DEAD (Google Drive 404), but `Parks Inspection Program - Element Tracking` (2jvr-j6ne) spells the same vocabulary out as element names - `"A" Drinking Fountain` 28,577 rows, `"C"` 17,301, `"E"` 13,611, `"D"` 11,670, `"B"` 5,080, `"F"` 1,953 - so A through F are drinking fountains in NYC Parks' own inspection language. That is an inference from two vocabularies matching rather than from NYC Parks stating it, and it is the one thing here a reader should treat as reasoned rather than measured. WHAT IS EXCLUDED AND WHY: Indoor Drinking Fountain 292 and Water Cooler 51 (not outdoors), Food Prep Sink 120, Slop Sink 27 and Bathroom Sink 11 (not for drinking), Trough 65 and Trough High Low 6 and Dog Fountain 1 (not for people), `Other` 53 (says nothing), and G 12, H 12, J 8 - the three letters with no counterpart in PIP's vocabulary, left out because nobody knows what they are rather than because anybody decided they are not fountains. https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1472 holds those 27 rows.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1452, which refused this layer as `unsuitable`; registered by https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1461 after the maintainer chose to ship it as unknown-status points rather than leave it held.
sources.notes: 3,195 rows ship. THE REFUSAL THIS REVERSES IS WORTH READING BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING HERE: nyc_water_holdback records why the layer was held, and only ONE of its two blockers is gone. The type problem is solved by the allowlist above. The status problem is NOT - `featuresta` still says Active about everything - and `confidence_floor` is what carries that rather than a filter, because there is no filter to write. The layer is also FOURTEEN MONTHS STALE (rowsUpdatedAt 2024-07-15) against the trails layer's monthly automation.
sources.boundary_source_comment: WHY A BOUNDARY AND NOT A WIDER RING (#1493). `NETWORK_BUFFER_FEET` asks how far this point is from a published trail line, which is the right question on a corridor and the wrong one in a city: in a park the PARK is the destination and the path through it is incidental. Measured 2026-09-15 against the UA release: the 500 ft ring admits 982 of 3,195 fountains and 249 of 975 restrooms, and in Central Park alone 182 of 221 points do not ship - 82% - with the losses falling on the Great Lawn, the Reservoir's outer edge and playgrounds set back from a drive. The ring is kept as an OR rather than replaced: 34 fountains ship today that are NOT inside any park boundary, near a line and outside a property, and a replacement would drop them. Measured the same day, 3,114 of 3,195 fountains sit inside one (97.5%), which is close to a blanket exemption for THIS source and is said plainly rather than dressed up - NYC Parks' fountains are, unsurprisingly, in NYC parks.

sources.title: NYC Parks Properties (park boundaries)
sources.url_comment: The portal page a reviewer reads, not the address the fetcher uses - that is `domain` plus `dataset_id`, exactly as on nyc_parks_trails.
sources.steward: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below - the same statutory grant that covers nyc_parks_trails, nyc_dot_greenways and the two NYC POI layers.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
sources.id_comment: THE SAME KEY THE FOUNTAINS ALREADY CARRY, which is what makes this a one-column join rather than a spatial guess. `nyc_drinking_fountains.gispropnum` and this layer's `gispropnum` are the same borough-letter property number, and the PIP inspection series (2jvr-j6ne, yg3y-7juh) keys `prop_id` the same way - see https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1483. The clip is still SPATIAL rather than by this key, deliberately: a point carrying a property number is not evidence it is inside that property's boundary, and the boundary is the thing being asserted.
sources.geometry_comment: POLYGONS, NOT POINTS, AND NOTHING DRAWS THEM. This layer exists to answer one question at export time - is this POI inside the park that publishes it - so it is never cut into tiles and never reaches a phone. The same shape oprhp_park_polygons has had since https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1371, where export_places.py reads boundaries for names and centroids and never ships the polygon itself.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1493, after https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1474 shipped the two NYC POI layers and the 500 ft ring was measured admitting 31% of the fountains and 26% of the restrooms.
sources.notes: 2,059 boundary polygons, measured live against the portal 2026-09-15. WHAT IT IS FOR: `boundary_source` on nyc_drinking_fountains and nyc_public_restrooms names this layer, and export_nearby_poi.clip_to_network keeps a POI that falls inside one of these boundaries however far it sits from a published trail line. Measured the same day: 3,114 of 3,195 fountains (97.5%) and 717 of 975 restrooms (73.5%) fall inside a boundary. THOSE TWO FIGURES DO DIFFERENT WORK - for restrooms the boundary discriminates, dropping 258 libraries, privately owned public spaces and transit entries; for fountains it is close to a blanket exemption, because NYC Parks' fountains are in NYC parks. WHAT IT IS NOT FOR: density. The worst default-visibility z12 screen was 55 pins before the NYC POI layers landed, 233 after, and 656 under this rule - all three measured with spike_oprhp_poi_density.py's own method over the published artifact. The maintainer's call of 2026-09-15, with those numbers in front of them, is that this is normal for New York City: POI_VISIBILITY.md's ~16 target and https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1105 were both derived for hiking zooms in wilderness, not for a borough. Density travels separately and POI_SITES.md's co-location clustering is what would answer it.
sources.reaches_hikers_comment: TRUE, THOUGH NO POLYGON IS PUBLISHED, on exactly oprhp_park_polygons' precedent: this layer decides which waypoints a hiker is shown, so it reaches them through the POIs it admits even though the boundaries themselves never leave the pipeline.

sources.title: NYC DOT Greenways (current, off-street)
sources.url_comment: The portal page, as on nyc_parks_trails - see that entry's url_comment.
sources.steward: New York City Department of Transportation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below, whose `author` is NYC Parks and which covers this entry too - one city, two agencies, and terms neither of them sets, because Local Law 11 of 2012 sets them for both. Named explicitly here because export_sources.py matches a licence block to an entry on `author` against `steward`, and those do not match for this one.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Transportation
sources.where_comment: THE FILTER IS THE WHOLE REASON THIS ENTRY IS DEFENSIBLE, and it is applied at the portal so the excluded rows are never fetched and never on disk. The dataset is DOT's entire bicycle network, 29,695 rows measured live 2026-09-15, of which the overwhelming majority is painted lanes in traffic. Each clause drops something specific. `status='Current'` drops 5,234 RETIRED rows - facilities that have been removed, which the dataset keeps deliberately as a historical record and which would be trail drawn where there is none. `grnwy='Greenway'` drops 23,358 rows that are ordinary bike lanes with no greenway designation at all. `onoffst='OFF'` drops a further 2,322 CURRENT greenway-designated rows that run ON STREET - the on-street connectors that link one off-street greenway to the next, signed as part of the route but carrying walkers into traffic. 3,039 rows survive all three. THE LAST CLAUSE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS FOR SAFETY and is the reason it is not enough to filter on the greenway flag: a hiker who reads a drawn line as a walking path and finds themselves on Queens Boulevard has been misled by this app, and CLAUDE.md's 'Four ways this app can hurt somebody' names in front of something dangerous as one of the four. Miss rather than cry wolf: the 2,322 dropped rows certainly include stretches that are pleasant to walk, and dropping them is the acceptable false negative.
sources.foot_comment: WHY A BICYCLE DATASET IS REGISTERED AT ALL, against the maintainer's decision of 2026-08-18 ('Only keep hiking trails for now... It's OurHike, not OurBike') - stated here rather than hoped past. That decision was taken over the per-use flag columns on OPRHP's and DEC's layers, where a row flagged BIKE and not FOOT is a mountain-bike trail: a different use of a different tread. This is not that. An off-street greenway is a shared-use PATH - the Manhattan waterfront esplanade, the Bronx River path, the Jamaica Bay trail - which people walk and run on in far greater numbers than they cycle, and which DOT happens to catalogue inside its bicycle-facility dataset because DOT's mandate for building them is a cycling one. The subject is the path; the dataset is the bicycle programme's record of it. WHERE THE INFERENCE IS, AND IT IS REAL: this layer has NO foot-use column. Nothing in it says a person may walk on a given segment, and `onoffst='OFF'` is being read as 'car-free, therefore walkable', which is this project's reading and not DOT's. @unvalidated. What would settle it is the NYC Parks layer, which covers the same ground for the 2,095 greenway segments whose `gwyjuris` is DPR and would corroborate walkability on those directly - a spatial join nobody has run - or, more cheaply, a maintainer who lives in the city walking one and saying. The reading errs toward including a paved path somebody might not want rather than excluding one they would, which is the opposite direction from the rest of this file, and is called out here for that reason.
sources.blaze_comment: No blaze field, and unlike nyc_parks_trails no colour hidden in a name either - greenways are signed with route markers rather than painted blazes, so the neutral here is a fact about the ground rather than a gap in the data.
sources.name_comment: `street` is the segment's own label and on greenway rows it carries the path's name rather than a road's - 'BRONX RIVER GREENWAY' on the sampled row, read live 2026-09-15. `gwsystem` is the coarser and more useful grouping if a screen wants one: Manhattan Waterfront 1,167, Jamaica Bay 799, Brooklyn Waterfront 690, Central Queens 614, Staten Island Waterfront 340, Historic Brooklyn 304, Queens Waterfront 302, Bronx River 243, Bronx Waterfront 233, Mosholu-Pelham 194, Hutchinson River 144, Eastern Queens 126 - counts over the 5,361 current greenway rows before the off-street clause, so they do not sum to the 3,039 that ship.
sources.duplicate_of_comment: THIS ENTRY IS THE JUNIOR OF A DECLARED DUPLICATE PAIR (#1459), and it is the first in this registry. Where a greenway segment is NYC Parks' own path drawn a second time, the Parks line survives and this one is removed; lib/duplicates.py holds the rule and the argument. WHY PARKS IS SENIOR: on the overlapping ground the land is theirs, so the land manager's own survey of its own ground is the better provenance - and where it carries no name, #1432's placeholder rule having left 3,777 parks rows nameless, the survivor inherits this entry's name rather than going unnamed. WHAT IT COSTS, MEASURED 2026-09-15 against both live layers: 427 of the 3,030 shipped greenway records removed, 30.35 miles, with 86 more coming near a parks trail for less than half their length and KEPT - which is the conservative rule working, because outside that overlap this entry is the only record of those paths. THE RULE VALIDATES ITSELF AGAINST #1453's CONTROL, which is why this is declared rather than argued: it pairs on geometry alone and never reads `gwyjuris`, yet 417 of the 427 it flags (97.7%) carry gwyjuris DPR - 22.9% of that jurisdiction's 1,823 segments against 1.4% of DOT's own 690 and 0.0% of all 517 rows belonging to NYSDOT, NPS, MTA, RIOC, NYSPRHP, GIPEC, BPCA, BBPDC, SBS, DCAS and private owners. Two independent methods landing on the same jurisdiction is the evidence that this removes double-draws rather than a dense city's near neighbours. The 10 DOT-jurisdiction flags sit just above #1453's 0.9% control floor and are not individually checked - @unvalidated, and what would settle it is standing on one.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1432, alongside nyc_parks_trails - see that entry. Found in the same NYC Open Data catalogue search; the greenway columns (grnwy, gwsystem, gwyjuris) are what made a bicycle dataset worth a second look rather than a skip.
sources.notes: 3,039 line segments come back after the `where` filter, out of 29,695 in the dataset, and 3,030 of them SHIP - measured live 2026-09-15 by running the fetched file through export_nearby_trails.build_records. The nine-row gap is the correction worth carrying rather than the round number: no row has a null geometry, which is what this note first said and is true, but nine carry a geometry OBJECT whose coordinates are empty, and keep_reason drops those as `no geometry`. A sentence that is literally true and still hides nine rows is the shape of claim CLAUDE.md asks this file to avoid. All the rest are MultiLineString in WGS84, and the filtered set returns in a single request. rowsUpdatedAt 2026-07-24. Fields kept include street/boro/gwsystem/gwsys2/gwyjuris/facilitycl/instdate/onoffst/status/grnwy. `gwyjuris` says who actually owns the path, across the whole current greenway set: DOT 3,667, DPR 2,095, NYSDOT 158, NPS 87, RIOC 81, MTA 63, NYSPRHP 45, GIPEC 39 - so a tenth of it is federal or state ground rather than the city's, and the NPS rows are Gateway National Recreation Area. WHY NOT THE ARCGIS COPY, since one exists and the existing fetcher could have read it with no new code: NYC DCP mirrors this dataset at services5.arcgis.com/GfwWNkhOj9bNBqoJ/arcgis/rest/services/Bike_Routes/FeatureServer/0, and probing it live 2026-09-15 gives editingInfo.dataLastEditDate 2017-03-08, 13,953 rows against the portal's 29,695, and a field list with NO grnwy, gwsystem, gwyjuris, status or ret_date - so the mirror is nine years stale AND structurally incapable of expressing the filter above, which is the difference between registering a greenway layer and registering every bike lane in New York as a walking path. That is NYC_SOURCE_SURVEY.md section 9's 'data.ny.gov copies - precedent, not a source' meeting a second city, and it is what made lib/socrata.py worth writing instead. OVERLAP WITH nyc_parks_trails IS EXPECTED AND UNMEASURED: 2,095 of the current greenway segments are DPR's, on park land the other layer also covers, so the same tread is plausibly drawn twice from two city agencies. Nobody has run the join. That is the concurrent-sources case NYC_SOURCE_SURVEY.md section 8's overlap table already collects for other ground, and it is recorded as open rather than assumed away.

sources.title: NYC Street Centerline - pedestrian ways (path, boardwalk, step street, non-vehicular)
sources.url_comment: The portal page a reviewer reads, not the address the fetcher uses - that is `domain` plus `dataset_id`, exactly as on nyc_parks_trails. SAME DATASET AS nyc_park_drives BELOW, registered twice on purpose: one dataset, two filters, two different grades of evidence, and a reviewer who can read either without the other. CSCL is the City Street Centerline - the road-bed file, whose pedestrian classes are the part this entry takes.
sources.steward: New York City Department of Transportation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below - the same statutory grant that covers nyc_parks_trails, nyc_dot_greenways and the two NYC POI layers. Named explicitly because export_sources.py matches a licence block to an entry on `author` against `steward`, and nyc_licence's author is NYC Parks rather than DOT - the same note nyc_dot_greenways carries.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Transportation
sources.blaze_comment: No blaze field and none to infer. A step street and a park promenade are signed with street signs where they are signed at all, so the neutral here is a fact about the ground rather than a gap in the data - the same reading nyc_dot_greenways' blaze_comment sets out.
sources.name_comment: CSCL's own label column, and it is populated rather than placeholdered - the nyc_parks_trails problem does not repeat here. What it carries is a STREET name applied to a walking way: `BRIDLE PATH`, `RESERVOIR LOOP`, `N MEADOW PATH`, `OCEAN PROM`, `UNION TURNPIKE PED AND BIKE PATH`. `UNNAMED ST` appears and is NOT declared a placeholder, because unlike `Unnamed Official Trail` it is not past NAMED_TRAIL_THRESHOLD_MILES and so cannot become a through-route feature; if it ever is, declare it here.
sources.where: status='2' AND (rw_type='5' OR rw_type='6' OR rw_type='7' OR (rw_type='1' AND trafdir='NV' AND posted_speed IS NULL AND number_travel_lanes IS NULL))
sources.where_comment: 6,498 rows of 5,990+101+246+162, measured live 2026-09-17, and EVERY CODE IN IT IS READ FROM NYC'S OWN DATA DICTIONARY rather than inferred. That dictionary is published as an ATTACHMENT on the dataset (Centerline.pdf, assetId 4cff63bb-aeb0-4ca3-adb5-d6027dc133d5) - not on the column descriptions, which are empty, and not at NYC Planning's PDF URL, which answers 403. Reading it is what turned this filter from a guess into a quotation, and it upgrades https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1530's @unvalidated reading of rw_type. RW_TYPE, quoted: 1 Street, 2 Highway, 3 Bridge, 4 Tunnel, 5 Boardwalk, 6 Path/Trail, 7 StepStreet, 8 Driveway, 9 Ramp, 10 Alley, 11 Unknown, 12 Non-Physical Street Segment, 13 U Turn, 14 Ferry Route. So 5/6/7 are the three classes the city itself calls pedestrian, and 6 alone is 5,990 rows. TRAFDIR, quoted: 'FT - With, TF - Against, TW - Two-Way, NV - Non-Vehicular'. STATUS, quoted: 1 Planned Private, 2 Constructed, 3 Paper, 4 Under Construction, 5 Demapped, 9 Paper Street Coincident with Boundary - so `status='2'` keeps only what is BUILT, and is the same guard nyc_dot_greenways' `status='Current'` clause provides against drawing a line where there is no tread. THE FOURTH CLAUSE IS THE ONE THAT NEEDED A SECOND TEST. `trafdir='NV'` alone is 580 rows and is NOT trustworthy on its own: 119 of those 580 carry a posted speed, which contradicts the non-vehicular assertion, and the names include HILLSIDE AVE, W END AVE, OCEAN AVE and REID AVE. Requiring posted_speed AND number_travel_lanes to be absent as well cuts it to 162, and what survives reads right - CENTRAL PARK GREAT HL 19, OCEAN PROM 15, UNION TURNPIKE PED AND BIKE PATH 13, BRUCKNER BOULEVARD BIKE PATH 11, CHERRY HILL PATH 4, COLUMBIA STREET ESPL 2, BAYONNE BR PED AND BIKE PATH 2. Two independent assertions agreeing is the bar this clause is held to, and one of them alone is not enough.
sources.duplicate_of_comment: NYC Parks' own trail record is senior to the street file's version of a path inside a park, which is the same precedence argument owned_route_names already makes for a route's steward. THE OTHER OVERLAP IS MEASURED AND NOT DECLARED, said rather than left for somebody to find: 1,023 of the 5,990 rw_type=6 names end in GREENWAY, so this layer and nyc_dot_greenways plainly describe some of the same tread, and `duplicate_of` takes ONE senior key per entry. Declaring the parks pair rather than the greenway pair is a choice about which overlap is larger inside a park, which is where this registration's purpose lies; the greenway overlap is left standing and is the open question, in the shape section 13 already collects. THE CHOICE IS NOW MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED, from the export's own dedupe line on 2026-09-17: this pair removes 698 duplicate records, 71.3 miles, at lib/duplicates.py's 10 m and half-length rule, with 121 more coming near a parks trail for less than half their length and kept. For comparison the nyc_dot_greenways pair, declared since #1459, removes 427 and 30.4 miles. So the pair this entry spends its one senior key on is the larger of the two by both counts, which is what the paragraph above was guessing at.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1533, out of https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1530 - the maintainer reported Central Park missing most of its paths, spike_central_park_paths.py measured nyc_parks_trails holding 6.98 of the park's 41-68 miles, and this is the layer that holds the rest. Found by reading NYC's own street file rather than by searching the catalogue again: CSCL is the road-bed centerline, and the question was whether a road-bed file says anything about walking. It says three things, and the data dictionary names all three.
sources.notes: 6,498 rows citywide, measured live 2026-09-17, and the reason this is registered is Central Park: 13.75 miles of rw_type=6 sit inside that park and 13.29 of them - 97% - lie more than 25 m from anything the build already draws, so this is path nobody had rather than a second copy of path somebody had. BRIDLE PATH 3.01 mi, RESERVOIR LOOP 1.59, N MEADOW PATH 1.58, BRIDLE PATH W 1.52, HECKSCHER BALLFIELDS PATH 1.29, E MEADOW PATH 0.86, CONSERVATORY GARDEN PATH 0.84. IT IS NOT A CENTRAL PARK FIX AND THAT IS THE POINT OF TAKING IT CITYWIDE: the same clip over Prospect Park returns 0.67 miles, because NYC Parks' own layer already covers Prospect at 96% of the two layers' combined mileage - this layer is thick exactly where that one is thin, and neither is a general substitute for the other. WHAT THE BOARDWALK AND STEP-STREET CLASSES ADD, on the maintainer's decision of 2026-09-17 taken with these counts in front of them: boardwalk is 101 rows and is Coney Island, Rockaway, Orchard Beach, Jacob Riis and the Manhattan Beach promenade; step street is 246 rows and is the Bronx and upper Manhattan public stairways plus 40 rows literally named PEDESTRIAN PATH, and on some hillsides it is the only pedestrian route there is. Both are pedestrian-only by the dictionary's own definition. THE ID PROBLEM nyc_parks_trails HAS DOES NOT REPEAT: CSCL publishes `physicalid` and lib/socrata.py promotes Socrata's `:id` besides, so nothing here falls back to a positional id. NO STATUS OR CLOSURE COLUMN beyond `status`, which is construction state rather than whether a path is walkable today, so every kept row exports as open and this export invents nothing.

sources.title: NYC park drives that are closed to cars (Central Park and Prospect Park)
sources.url_comment: The same dataset as nyc_cscl_paths above and a separate entry on purpose. THE TWO ENTRIES REST ON DIFFERENT EVIDENCE AND A READER HAS TO BE ABLE TO SEE WHICH IS WHICH: that one quotes the city's own dictionary, this one contradicts the city's own columns on a maintainer's say-so. Merging them into one filter would bury the second fact inside the first one's credibility.
sources.steward: New York City Department of Transportation
sources.licence: See nyc_licence below - the same statutory grant, and see nyc_cscl_paths' licence note for why the block is named here rather than matched on `steward`.
sources.attribution: New York City Department of Transportation
sources.where: status='2' AND rw_type='1' AND ((boroughcode='1' AND stname_label in('EAST DR','WEST DR','CENTER DR','TERRACE DR')) OR (boroughcode='3' AND stname_label in('EAST DR','WEST DR','CENTER DR','WELLHOUSE DR','S LAKE DR','E LAKE DR')))
sources.where_comment: 124 rows, measured live 2026-09-17. THE NAMES ARE A REVIEWED LIST AND NOT A RULE, which is the whole difference between this entry and nyc_cscl_paths. Central Park is boroughcode 1 and Prospect Park is 3; the four Central Park names are its ring drives and the six Brooklyn names are Prospect Park's ring plus its interior lake and Wellhouse drives. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: Central Park's 65/79/86/97 St TRANSVERSES, 2.89 miles in the same rw_type, excluded by the maintainer on 2026-09-17 in as many words - they carry through traffic in a sunken cut and are not walkable. Queens (boroughcode 4) has its own EAST DR, WEST DR and CENTER DR in Flushing Meadows and they are NOT here, which is why the clause is keyed on borough rather than on name alone. `boundary_source` below is what removes the rest of the leak; the name list alone is not sufficient and was measured not to be.
sources.boundary_source_comment: WHY A NAME LIST IS NOT ENOUGH, measured 2026-09-17 before this key was added rather than after a reviewer asked. Clipping each (borough, name) pair to NYC Parks' own boundary polygon shows four of the ten leaking outside the park they are named for: boro 3 EAST DR by 0.30 mi over 7 segments, boro 1 TERRACE DR by 0.03, boro 3 WEST DR by 0.02, boro 3 CENTER DR by 0.04. Small, and on a safety path a tenth of a mile of city street drawn as a car-free park drive is the failure this whole entry is trying not to commit. So the boundary does the final cut and the name list only proposes candidates. The same `boundary_source` key export_nearby_poi.py already reads for a POI inside a park property (#1493); `boundary_names` is new and narrows it to the two parks whose drives are reviewed, because the concept 'a street inside any park is walkable' is exactly what the measurement below refutes.
sources.discovered_via: https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/1533, decision 2. The maintainer asked for every NYC park rather than Central Park alone, and asked whether the driveable ones could be identified and excluded mechanically.
sources.notes: 12.02 miles across 124 segments: Central Park 6.61 (EAST DR 2.90, WEST DR 2.73, CENTER DR 0.58, TERRACE DR 0.40) and Prospect Park 5.41 (WEST DR 1.96, EAST DR 1.46, CENTER DR 0.68, WELLHOUSE DR 0.60, S LAKE DR 0.48, E LAKE DR 0.11). THIS ENTRY CONTRADICTS ITS OWN SOURCE AND THAT HAS TO BE SAID FIRST. CSCL still models these as vehicular streets: EAST DR reads trafdir FT with posted_speed 20 and one travel lane, WEST DR reads TF/TW at 25, TERRACE DR reads TW at 25 with three lanes. Central Park's and Prospect Park's drives were closed to cars in 2018 and the street file has not caught up, so drawing them as walkable is OURS rather than the city's, and it is the one place in this registry where a display is deliberately allowed to outrun its source. THE EVIDENCE IS THE MAINTAINER'S, recorded as that and not dressed up: their decision of 2026-09-17, made as somebody who lives in New York City and named this park as the ground they can test on (#1432). @unvalidated against any published source - the city's own pages answer 403 from an agent sandbox, so nobody in this repository has read a primary document saying these are car-free. What would settle it: a DOT or NYC Parks page stating the closure, cited here by URL and date, or a CSCL republication that finally sets these rows to trafdir NV. WHY THE MECHANICAL ROUTE WAS TRIED FIRST AND REJECTED, so it is not tried again: `trafdir='NV'` is the city's own non-vehicular assertion and it finds only 3.59 miles inside all 2,061 park polygons - 0.24 of it in Prospect Park and NONE of Central Park's four drives - against 61.58 miles of park-interior street the city marks vehicular. nyc_dot_greenways carries none of these drives. NYC's Open Streets layer (uiay-nctu, 391 rows) is a per-day schedule of temporary closures on ordinary streets, not a permanent status, and reading a Sunday-morning closure as a walkable path would be worse than omitting one. So there is no NYC dataset that says which park drives are car-free, and a reviewed list is the honest mechanism rather than a lazy one. WHY EVERY OTHER PARK IS OUT, which was the maintainer's actual question: a rule admitting any street inside a park boundary takes 61.58 miles across 79 parks, and the measurement says what that buys - Pelham Bay's ORCHARD BEACH BUS TERMINAL LOOP and ORCHARD BEACH ROAD, Bronx Park's JUNGLE WORLD RD and BOTANICAL GARDEN RD (zoo and garden service roads), Flushing Meadows' SHEA RD and MERIDIAN RD, Forest Park's FOREST PARK DR, Highland Park's HIGHLAND BLVD. Those carry cars, and a hiker walked onto one is CLAUDE.md's third way this app can hurt somebody. Adding a park here is one reviewed row and a measurement, and the file is built so that is cheap.

sources.title: Trails in National Park Service units (nationwide)
sources.licence: PUBLIC DOMAIN, on 17 U.S.C. 105 and the maintainer's adoption of it for usfs_trails (2026-09-02). A work prepared by an officer or employee of the U.S. Government as part of their official duties is not subject to domestic copyright, so there is nothing here for the agency to grant or withhold - which is why this is `stated_by_org` rather than `maintainer_authorisation`, on usfs_trails' own reasoning.
sources.discovered_via: Catalogued by the #1543 research pass into reference/trail_orgs.json, then PROBED for #1778 on 2026-09-30 - the catalogue never opened these URLs, so every figure in `notes` is this probe's and not its. Registered by hand: discover_sources.py walks ATC's Experience Builder app and none of these sit behind it.
sources.notes: 31,485 polyline features, 42 fields, measured 2026-09-30 by querying the layer (returnCountOnly, and the layer's own metadata for the rest). Published in EPSG:3857. maxRecordCount 2,000, which is what a paged fetch has to respect. A 504 from the server on the first probe attempt; the retry answered, and that is recorded as a retry rather than as a finding about the layer.
sources.reaches_hikers_comment: Registered, not shipped - features/ORG_BULK_LOAD.md's batches 2 and 3, which register before they ship on purpose. The flip is batch 4 and its own decision; it wants a UA publish first, to show the pipeline carries 2.67x the features it carries today.
sources.blaze_comment: Declared so network_line_sources() reads this layer at all (#1787): that selector is `'blaze_field' in s or 'blaze_default' in s`, and a trail-line source carrying neither is skipped exactly as OPRHP's facilities points are. `reaches_hikers` gates publish.py and is a different question - #1786 flipped it alone and this layer still reached nobody. 'Unknown' is what usfs_trails and the four NYC layers already use for a steward publishing no blaze. EVERY FIELD OF THIS LAYER WAS READ LIVE on 2026-09-30 rather than pattern-matched, because #1778's probe used a name filter and a filter only finds what it was told to look for. `TRLCLASS` is the trail's construction standard, not a blaze.

sources.title: NPS Alerts, for the park codes the clubs draw on
sources.licence: PUBLIC DOMAIN, on 17 U.S.C. 105, the reading nps_trails ships on and the reason this is `stated_by_org` rather than `maintainer_authorisation` (usfs_trails' own reasoning). NPS's website disclaimer, as the decision 53 inventory quoted it (batch 5, 2026-10-03) from https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/disclaimer.htm: "material created by the National Park Service and presented on this website, unless otherwise indicated, is generally considered in the public domain." NPS's developer terms were not read: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/developer/terms-of-service.htm answered 404 to the inventory (batch 2, 2026-10-03), so whether they say anything about a scheduled reader is @unvalidated. What publishes is decision 53's facts and a link (features/ORG_NOTICES.md §7): title, category, park, date and the link, never the description.
sources.api_key_comment: developer.nps.gov is api.data.gov's gateway, which refuses a request with no key (it answered /robots.txt itself with 403 `API_KEY_MISSING`, the decision 53 inventory, 2026-10-03). The extract reads the key from the NPS_API_KEY environment variable (extract/_json_apis.py's NPS_API_KEY_ENV) and sends it as the `X-Api-Key` header, never in a URL; unset, the resource is `unavailable` and its table is withdrawn, never read as no alerts (extract/_json_apis.py). A key is free from https://www.nps.gov/subjects/developer/get-started.htm. The public demonstration key allows 10 requests an hour (`x-ratelimit-limit: 10`, measured by the inventory) and is never used by a scheduled job.
sources.park_codes_comment: Each NPS park code a club folder draws on, and those folders by trail_orgs.json slug: the one home for both. The extract asks for every code here in one request (`parkCode=` takes a comma-separated list, measured by the inventory as one call of 10 codes, batch 3), and dbt assigns each club its portion from this map (decision 34). Twenty-five of the codes come from the decision 53 inventory's live reads (batches 1 to 5, 2026-10-03); `appa` and `dewa` come from amc_dv/closures.py's note, and `grsm` for nc-mst from nc_mst/warnings.py's, read 2026-10-01. The atc/ and amc_dv/ files are left as they are (ATC's own resources, and a note drawn from atc/), so those two codes reach dbt through this map alone. WHAT THIS LIST LEAVES OUT: nps/ and nps_poi/ are national (nps_trails holds 31,485 features across every unit, and the API's national list held 622 alerts on 2026-10-03), and every unit not named here is not read. Deleting this field would not read them either: the resource refuses an entry with no codes, because a national read is a decision for the maintainer (two pages of about 500 an hour), not a default.

freshness.notes: No ETag and no Last-Modified on the API's answers (decision 53 inventory, every batch, 2026-10-03), so nothing can say FRESH: every hourly run reads the listed codes, one request of up to NPS_PAGE_SIZE alerts, paged by `start` if the answer is longer. The answer's own `total` (a string) is the count that proves a zero, read in the same response as the rows.

sources.notes: Fields per alert (measured on the national list's first 50, 2026-10-03): id (a GUID, unique on 50 of 50), url (empty on 31 of 50), title, parkCode, description, category (Park Closure 25, Caution 11, Information 8, Danger 6), relatedRoadEvents (a list of {title, id, type, url}), lastIndexedDate ('2026-10-02 00:00:00.0', an index date, not a start or an end). No geometry: a park code is the place, so `place` stays unplaced unless a reviewed term says otherwise. Category alone does not decide obstructs_trail: a Park Closure most often closes a facility or a road, not a trail (semo's two, 2026-10-03, close visitor centres). One resource, in nps/warnings.py; the closures staging model reads it too, since nps/closures.py now claims the park closure layers (decision 53 phase B) and a file takes one form.

sources.key_comment: `guid`: present and unique on all 9 items read 2026-10-04, the feed's own id for an episode, which a podcast app keys on too.

sources.title: NPS audio (the API's /multimedia/audio, national)
sources.licence: PUBLIC DOMAIN, on 17 U.S.C. 105, the reading nps_trails and nps_alerts ship on: NPS's website disclaimer, as decision 53's inventory quoted it (batch 5, 2026-10-03) from https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/disclaimer.htm, "material created by the National Park Service and presented on this website, unless otherwise indicated, is generally considered in the public domain." NPS's developer terms were not read (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/developer/terms-of-service.htm answered 404 to that inventory), so whether they say anything about a scheduled reader is @unvalidated.
sources.api_key_comment: developer.nps.gov is api.data.gov's gateway, which refuses a request with no key. The extract reads the key from NPS_API_KEY (extract/_json_apis.py's NPS_API_KEY_ENV), the secret nps_alerts already uses, and sends it as the `X-Api-Key` header, never in a URL; unset, the resource is `unavailable` and its table withdrawn, never read as an empty list. Section C measured these lists with api.data.gov's public DEMO_KEY (10 requests an hour, `x-ratelimit-limit: 10`), by hand, once; no job uses it.
sources.person_fields_comment: Decision 59, Reasoned: an oral history's `transcript` is a named private individual's own account of their life (the first item read on 2026-10-04 was one), so the column never loads for any item; the title and description say what a clip is. `credit` (a collection's or a narrator's line) lands as NPS states it.
sources.key_comment: `id`, NPS's own GUID for each item: present and unique on the 2 rows of a sample read on 2026-10-04; the full read was refused by the public DEMO_KEY's shared hourly limit (HTTP 429 OVER_RATE_LIMIT, 08:42 UTC). The reader itself raises on a missing or repeated id within a read (extract/_content.py's NpsContent), so a landed table is unique on it by construction; that the whole list is, and that the id is stable from one read to the next, is @unvalidated until the first monthly run under NPS_API_KEY reads every row and re-measures it.

freshness.notes: No ETag and no Last-Modified on the API's answers (decision 53's inventory, every batch, and section C's reads of 2026-10-04), so nothing can say FRESH: every monthly run reads the list, 500 a page, and the answer's own `total` is the count that proves a zero.

sources.blaze_comment: Declared so network_line_sources() reads this layer at all (#1787): that selector is `'blaze_field' in s or 'blaze_default' in s`, and a trail-line source carrying neither is skipped exactly as OPRHP's facilities points are. `reaches_hikers` gates publish.py and is a different question - #1786 flipped it alone and this layer still reached nobody. 'Unknown' is what usfs_trails and the four NYC layers already use for a steward publishing no blaze. EVERY FIELD OF THIS LAYER WAS READ LIVE on 2026-09-30 rather than pattern-matched, because #1778's probe used a name filter and a filter only finds what it was told to look for.

sources.discovered_via: The Laurel Ridge alerts page's `data-api-url`, found by pipeline/ELT.md decision 53's phase A inventory (batch 1), registered in phase B.
sources.notes: An item is {IsAlert: bool, Message: HTML} and nothing else: no title, no date, no id (measured 2026-10-03). The extract keys each by a sha256 of its park id and text (advisory_key in extract/_json_apis.py), so an edited advisory is a new row, and decision 52's _first_seen_at is the only date it will have. LIVE SAFETY ITEM, 2026-10-03: Laurel Ridge's answer carries IsAlert true, "The unnamed tributary between mile-marker 24 and 25 has been contaminated by lead and other heavy metals. Please do not use this as a drinking water source." That is a water fact at an LHHT mile, and belongs on the water path as well as in warnings. The other three Laurel Ridge items are statewide (drones, spotted lanternfly, firewood).
sources.reaches_hikers_comment: Held, decision 63's hold (2026-10-04): an advisory is only {IsAlert, Message}, and the Message is DCNR's own wording, which decision 55 keeps out of every mart, so a published row would be a notice with no title, no link and no place but a park id. Laurel Ridge's lead-contaminated tributary (miles 24 to 25) is a water fact for a reviewed water note, not this. Settled by a title and a place the advisory's own fields can give.

sources.discovered_via: The coverage audit's ouachita warnings note (gid 866760807, 2026-10-01), re-read by pipeline/ELT.md decision 53's phase A inventory (batch 1, as xlsx) and as CSV in phase B, 2026-10-03.
sources.notes: Read 2026-10-03 as CSV: 184 segment rows in four tables (the Ouachita Trail, Black Fork Wilderness, Eagle Rock Loop and the Womble Trail), each under its own title row and `Sect` header, then a colour legend and a disclaimer. Key: (table_title, sect, begin_mile, end_mile), unique on 184 of 184. Eleven columns; two of them, 'Adopted by' and 'Source of Last Condition Report', name people and never load: the extract keeps an allow list of the other nine (extract/_json_apis.py's SHEET_COLUMNS). WHAT THE CSV LOSES, and the coverage audit said so first ('read the xlsx, not the CSV, or the one field that says "treacherous" is lost'): each segment's condition is its cells' fill colour, by the sheet's own legend green clear, yellow some impediment, red difficult to follow, gray no current report, plus blue and orange; a CSV holds values only. The xlsx export keeps the fills and needs a spreadsheet reader (openpyxl) the extract job does not install, which is the maintainer's call. Until then the condition a hiker most needs from this sheet does not land.
sources.reaches_hikers_comment: Held, decision 63's hold (2026-10-04): each segment's condition is its cells' fill colour, which the CSV does not carry, so all 184 segments, clear ones included, would publish as warnings, none with a geometry. Settled by the xlsx export its notes name (a spreadsheet reader, the maintainer's call) and a reviewed placing of its miles.

sources.notes: One of the five WordPress categories FTA files its closures and Notices to Hikers under (ids 37, 40, 41, 42 and 43; X-WP-Total 14 under all five, 2026-10-03), read through the category's RSS feed. The REST posts route would be the complete list, but it serves each post's rendered content, and that content carries staff e-mail addresses and a phone number (measured 2026-10-03), which decision 59 keeps out whole; the feed reader lands no prose and no person. Each category held 1 to 5 posts, fewer than a feed's 10, so each feed was the whole category on the day it was read, and is still a window. The categories mix closures with NTH, so an unclassified row goes to warnings (decision 7), and old posts stay published (a 2018 bear policy), so expiry is a dbt rule. Read live at 2026-10-03T22:11:10Z under lib/user_agent.py's agent, robots.txt allows the path for our agent, no Crawl-delay: HTTP 200, 7,767 bytes, Last-Modified Sat, 03 Oct 2026 18:45:31 GMT. Through FeedNotices that answer lands 2 rows, one an item, `item_id` taken from the guid on 2 and distinct on 2 of 2: the key. The item's licenseInfo and accessInformation are empty and the layer carries no copyrightText (read 2026-10-03), so the layer rests on decision 21a's presumption for a GIS layer an organization publishes itself, anonymously, on a public endpoint (`public_gis`; pipeline/ELT.md, 'Who may publish', rule 3). IT IS NOT A LICENCE FROM GMC and must never be rendered as one.
sources.discovered_via: pipeline/reference/org_coverage.json's gmc points_of_interest row (AVAILABLE_NOT_LOADED in the coverage audit, 2026-10-01), read again live for decision 54's wave 1 on 2026-10-03: robots.txt first, lib/user_agent.py's agent, two seconds or more between requests to one host, and the layer's metadata, returnCountOnly count, item and per-value counts read. Registered by hand.
sources.person_fields_comment: `SOURCE` names who collected each point on GMC's layers: on OS_MASTER a GPS collector's name on 29 rows (two staff members, each by first initial and surname) beside 'ATC Asset Inventory 2019*' 29, and on PARKING_MASTER a staff member's name on 1 (grouped 2026-10-03; the names are not copied here). It is listed here so it is never asked for; the layer's other columns load. On this layer Source is blank on all 164.
sources.notes: 164 points, 20 fields, last edited 2026-08-31 (editingInfo, read 2026-10-03). Three 0/1 flags rather than one type: VISTA 108, SUMMIT 75, TOWER 3; VSTYPE is blank on all 164. KEY: GlobalID, 164 distinct of 164; Name is not (134).
sources.reaches_hikers_comment: True from 2026-10-04 (decision 63: a layer reaches hikers once its rules are in dbt and tested). int_points_of_interest__club_points types its points from the club_poi_types seed (viewpoint), an allowlist by the code the layer lands, each rule a unit test in _points_of_interest__club_points.yml; the classifier, int_sources__publication, the 500 ft ring around the published network and the dedupe then run over it as over every other organization's points. new_data_report.py counts what it adds.

sources.date_fields_comment: The layer's esriFieldTypeDate fields, read off its metadata on 2026-10-03 by decision 54's wave 1 trail-line read. They land as epoch milliseconds (extract/_kinds.py's ESRI_TYPES), and the base model casts each to a UTC timestamp.
sources.person_fields_comment: creator and editor hold DNR staff accounts; entityaddress, entityphone and entityemail are each managing entity's contact details, and entityemail holds individuals' e-mail addresses on many rows (read 2026-10-03). None of the five ever loads, and the three entity fields have ordinary names, so they are listed.

freshness.notes: An on-prem server, so no ArcGIS Online 304: extract/_kinds.py's statistics fingerprint is count and max of the object id with max(editdate), editor tracking's own edit date (read 2026-10-03).

oprhp_licence._comment: The basis on which the four oprhp_* layers above may be fetched, and the bar their data has to clear before any of it is republished to hikers. CORRECTED 2026-08-24 (#950). THAT WAS WRONG, and the way it was wrong is worth recording: the licenseInfo was read through a 200-character truncation on 2026-08-18, which cut off exactly at the sentence where the disclaimer ends and the actual terms begin. Reuse is permitted; attribution to OPRHP is REQUIRED on 'any maps, reports, or other materials created using OPRHP data'; and the data is provided 'for informational and NON-COMMERCIAL purposes'. The second condition is the one that needs a human: features/PRICING_MODEL.md designs a paid thru-hike pass and regional passes, so whether shipping these lines inside OurHike is a non-commercial use is a judgement about the product, not a fact about the layer. The reading that says yes is PRICING_MODEL.md's own pricing value #5 - the trail line is in the tier that 'stay[s] free forever, for everyone, regardless of ability to pay', and what is sold is the convenience layer above it. That reading is not recorded here as settled, because nobody with authority to settle it has written it down.

THE REASONING, recorded because a determination nobody can inspect is worth no more than an assertion: features/PRICING_MODEL.md's pricing value #1 keeps the core map, water, shelters, GPS, elevation, closures and warnings 'free forever, for everyone, regardless of ability to pay', and a trail line is squarely in that tier. nynjtc_hikes_licence._comment: The basis on which NYNJTC's Favorite Hikes - their prose, their photographs and their categorisation - may be fetched AND republished to hikers, whole. A FOURTH block for NYNJTC rather than a widening of nynjtc_licence (the two trail extracts), nynjtc_notices_licence (the alerts) or nynjtc_guide_licence (the Long Path section guide), because each of those says it must not be read as precedent for anything else NYNJTC publishes, and honouring that sentence means the hikes needed their own answer. THEY HAVE ONE, AND IT IS BROADER THAN THE OTHER THREE, which is the thing to be precise about. The maintainer's ask on 2026-09-08 came with the permission in the same sentence - 'add all the Hikes from https://www.nynjtc.org/favorite-hikes/ to this (we have their permission) ... Include everything, the description, the photos' - and when asked on 2026-09-09 what the permission covers, answered 'We can use anything'. Every other NYNJTC block here ships FACTS and a link and stops short of the prose; this one ships the prose and the pictures, on the maintainer's word that NYNJTC has said so. Recorded in those words because the basis is the maintainer relaying NYNJTC's permission and carrying the consequence; NYNJTC's own written grant is not in this repository, and a reader should know that from this block rather than infer it. IT IS NOT A LICENCE TO SUBLICENSE THEIR WORK ONWARD, and the attribution is a condition rather than a courtesy: every photograph ships with the credit line the page carries ('Photo by Daniel Chazin', 'Photo: Jane Daniels'), every hike names the New York-New Jersey Trail Conference as its author and links to their page, and a photograph the page does not credit is not fetched at all (fetch_nynjtc_hikes.py). WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER, because the permission was for their hikes and these are not theirs: the Avenza map links, excluded on the maintainer's instruction ('Leave Avenza out'); the 39 password-protected hikes, which sit behind NYNJTC's own gate and were not asked for ('just do the 20 public ones'); and the ROUTE, which NYNJTC does not publish - they publish a trailhead pin and a description, and the line a hiker sees is OurHike's construction from that description over this build's own trail lines, reviewed by the maintainer, and the card says so. THE SAFETY HOLDBACKS IT DOES NOT TOUCH, because a licence answer is not a safety answer: no route ships until a person has signed off its ends in reference/nynjtc_hike_routes.json; a hike whose ground this build has no lines for is held rather than approximated; the miles and climb a card prints are measured on this build's lines beside NYNJTC's own stated length, never one dressed as the other; and a climb the elevation sidecar cannot price is absent, never zero. Those come from the exporter and the review, not from this block, and this block cannot loosen them. WHAT CHANGED ON 2026-09-15 (#1427): the ROAD, not the permission. `nynjtc_favorite_hikes` - the twenty public write-ups read off nynjtc.org's WordPress API - is no longer registered and is no longer fetched; the maintainer supplied NYNJTC's full list as an export they host themselves and asked for the scrape to stop ('Can you load all the hikes from here, and stop scraping the website'). `nynjtc_hike_finder` is that road and inherits every word of this block, which is why the block outlived the source entry that first needed it. Two things the export adds that nynjtc.org never had: 385 hikes instead of 20, because the password gate this licence declined to walk through is not in front of them; and a GPX track for 113 of them - a line the publisher DREW rather than a survey anybody walked, corrected 2026-09-15 under #1451 and measured in nynjtc_hike_finder's notes - which is the first route in this repository that NYNJTC's hikes did not need OurHike to construct. The paragraph above about the route being OurHike's construction is therefore true of 272 of the 385 and false of the other 113, and the artifact says which is which in `routeProvenance`.

atc_support._comment: How a hiker supports the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, and the bounds on where OurHike may say so (#932). THE PRODUCT COMMITMENT THIS SCHEMA EXISTS TO KEEP: OurHike links out and never holds the money. A block that can express nothing but a destination, a call to action and a permission is the cheapest way to keep that true - there is no field here that could hold a payment processor, an amount, or a share, and adding one should read as the product change it would be. Separate from #107 - Web-only donation/payment flow, which is about OurHike taking money and is deliberately a different thing. WHERE THE WORDS COME FROM: `donate_cta` is ATC's own button, read verbatim from their page on 2026-08-27, not a house string - a trail conservancy and a state parks department do not ask for support in the same voice, and flattening them into one button is the app speaking for an organization it does not represent. There is NO `donate_blurb` here, and its absence is the same rule the notices ship on: a destination and a button label are facts about an organization, a paragraph about what the money does is that organization's writing, and #458's facts-and-a-link split says OurHike carries the first and links to the second. It arrives when ATC sends words, not when somebody lifts them.

WHICH PAGE, AND WHOSE WORDS: nynjtc.org's own navigation links the store's map collection under the text 'Trail Maps', read live 2026-09-17, and that is `store_cta` verbatim - never a house string. `referral` is a query string appended to every link out, so NYNJTC's own Shopify reports can count what arrived from this app; OurHike sees none of it, which is the same commitment the donate line keeps (money and measurement both stay on the org's side). `paper_maps` names the reviewed table of products, sheets and the parks each sheet covers, in NYNJTC's own spelling. oprhp_support._comment: How a hiker supports New York State's parks, and THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS ENTRY THAT MUST NOT BE SMOOTHED OVER (#932): the money does not go to the steward this block is joined to. NYS OPRHP is a state agency and has no donation destination of its own. The 'Donate' link on parks.ny.gov points at the NATURAL HERITAGE TRUST, a separate 501(c)(3) that is the parks system's philanthropic partner - a different legal organization from the one whose trail lines and closures this registry ships. Recording it as OPRHP's donate link and rendering 'Support NYS OPRHP' over it would tell a hiker their money reaches the agency, which is not what happens. So `donate_cta` is the state's own word and `donate_recipient` names who actually receives it, and any surface rendering this block MUST render the recipient too - that is what `donate_recipient` is for, and it is the reason this block is not simply the other two with a different URL. Same rule as everywhere else in this repository: never let a display outrun its source.

org_marks._comment: Whether each organization has granted OurHike the right to SHIP ITS OWN ORG MARK - its logo on a steward card - and the answer for every one of them today is no (#933). A TRAIL MARK is a different question with a different answer, and the two were run together until the maintainer's decision of 2026-09-30; see `trail_marks` below. WHY AN ORG MARK IS STILL A LICENCE QUESTION: OurHike is offline-first, so an org's logo is not fetched when a card renders - it is copied into the download and carried on a hiker's phone, potentially for months, inside an application distributed under AGPL-3.0. That is redistribution. A logo is usually held MORE tightly than the data: trademark rather than copyright, with organizations that care a great deal about how their mark is used, and a steward card is the surface where a logo reads as endorsement. WHY THE BLOCK EXISTS WHILE IT IS EMPTY OF GRANTS. The record has to be older than the first asset, or the first asset arrives with the question already forgotten. tests/test_org_marks.py is what makes this block bite: it derives the org list from the registry's own providers, so a newly registered organization cannot slip past by not being added to a second place, and it FAILS if an ORG mark asset exists in the client tree for an org whose state here is not `granted`. AN ORG MARK SLOT RENDERS EMPTY UNTIL A GRANT ARRIVES - never a placeholder mark, never an initial, never a generated shape. That last sentence used to govern trail marks too, and the maintainer reversed it on 2026-09-30: see `trail_marks._comment` for what replaced it and why.

state_vocabulary.not_asked: Nobody has put the question to this organization. The default, and not a judgement about whether they would say yes.
state_vocabulary.asked: The ask has been sent and no answer has come back. Carries `asked_date` so a silence can be aged rather than forgotten.
state_vocabulary.granted: The organization has given permission in writing. Carries every field in `required_on_grant` below, and is the ONLY state under which a mark asset may exist in the tree.
state_vocabulary.refused: The organization has said no. Recorded rather than deleted, so nobody asks twice and nobody assumes the silence in `not_asked` means this.

permission_meanings.redistribute_in_offline_bundle: The mark may be copied into a downloadable map package and carried on a hiker's phone offline, inside an AGPL-3.0 application. This is the permission that makes the others necessary.
permission_meanings.display_beside_own_attribution: The mark appears beside the organization's own attribution string and never detached from it, so a mark can never read as an endorsement of something the org did not publish.
permission_meanings.no_modification: Not recoloured, not cropped, not composited, not redrawn at a size the org did not supply. `asset` records what they sent; the app renders that.
permission_meanings.brand_colour_chip_only: A brand colour may tint the organization's chip and NOTHING ELSE - above all never a trail line. The map's hue channel means WHICH BLAZE A HIKER FOLLOWS (features/TRAIL_BLAZE_COLORS.md), so an organization's brand colour touching a trail line would make the map say something false about paint on a tree. This is the one permission that is a constraint on OurHike rather than a grant from the org, and it is recorded here because it is the one an implementer is most likely to breach by accident.

claim_vocabulary.unclaimed: The steward has not been in touch about this mark. The default. It does NOT mean nobody asked and it does NOT mean permission - it means OurHike is identifying their trail with their own marker and has left them an obvious way to take it back.
claim_vocabulary.claimed: The steward has been in touch and is content for the mark to ship. Carries `claimed_date` and `claimed_via` so the word rests on something. Not the same as an org-mark grant above, which is a different asset on a different surface.
claim_vocabulary.withdrawn: The steward asked for the mark to come out. The row STAYS - deleting it would let the next sweep re-add the file - and `test_a_withdrawn_mark_is_gone_from_the_tree` fails while the asset is still there. Carries `withdrawn_date` and `withdrawn_reason`.

trail_marks._comment: THE STEWARD'S OWN TRAIL MARKER, SHIPPED BY DEFAULT. The maintainer's decision of 2026-09-30, reversing this file's earlier rule that a mark slot renders empty until a grant arrives. WHAT CHANGED AND WHY. The earlier rule was written for ORG marks - a logo on a steward card, where it reads as endorsement - and was then applied to trail markers too, which is a different thing on a different surface. A trail marker on a map badge identifies WHICH TRAIL THE LINE IS. That is what the marker is for: it is the same symbol nailed to the trees a hiker is walking past, and every paper map, guidebook and trail app shows it for the same reason. Withholding it did not protect anybody - it left a hiker unable to tell the A.T. from the six other red lines on the screen, which is the first of the four ways this app can hurt somebody (CLAUDE.md: lost). OPT-OUT, NOT OPT-IN. Every mark here ships unclaimed. A steward who wants it gone says so and the row goes `withdrawn`, which turns the suite red until the file is out of the tree - so the promise is enforced by CI rather than by anybody remembering. A steward who is happy says so and the row goes `claimed`. Neither state is required for the mark to ship, and `unclaimed` is not a claim that anybody granted anything. WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER. It is the trail's marker, on the trail-identifying surfaces this app draws - the map badge and the line sheet - at the ~18-20px these render at. Not an org logo on a steward card (that is `orgs` above, still opt-in). Not merchandise, not marketing, not a claim of affiliation or endorsement, and not a licence to sublicense onward. TWO ROWS ARE ABSENT ON PURPOSE AND ONE ARRIVED BY A DIFFERENT DOOR. `pohe` and `natr` ship nothing: their markers are prescribed in the Federal Register and are federal insignia under 18 U.S.C. 701. AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS PARAGRAPH SAID 'one row' AND NAMED THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST AND NORTH COUNTRY AS THE PAIR CARRYING ASSOCIATION MARKS INSTEAD, AND BOTH HALVES WERE WRONG - the count was two, and the Pacific Northwest has no Federal Register notice at all. What is true: North Country ships NCTA's blue map icon and Pacific Northwest ships PNTA's roundel, neither of which is a prescribed marker. See `_the_nst_shield_question` below for the part that is NOT resolved. THE PCT ROW IS NOT PCTA'S FILE AND MUST NOT BE READ AS ONE. PCTA's media page still states in terms that the PCT emblem, the PCT diamond and the PCTA logo each need written permission, and nobody has written - nothing here touches that. What ships is the US FOREST SERVICE's own copy of the trail emblem, off the agency that administers the trail, so the mark rests on 17 U.S.C. 105 rather than on the opt-out decision above. See the `pct` row for the three separate questions that answer had to clear, one of which is not a copyright question at all. Provenance for every row is pipeline/reference/trail_marks.json, which holds the URL each was fetched from, its pixel size and its measured ink at 18px. The images here are resized copies - see `scope` on each row.

pct.basis: PUBLIC DOMAIN, not the opt-out decision the other 33 rows carry. The US Forest Service administers the Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail and publishes this emblem on its own trail page; a work of the US government carries no copyright (17 U.S.C. 105), which is the same basis reference/trail_orgs.json's `usfs` row already records for this publisher's data. THREE QUESTIONS, AND THE FIRST ONE ONLY ANSWERS COPYRIGHT. (1) Copyright: answered above. (2) Official insignia, which 17 U.S.C. 105 does NOT answer - 18 U.S.C. 701 protects trail markers prescribed by the Interior Department, and that is why `pohe` and `natr` ship nothing. (An earlier version of this sentence also claimed the North Country and New England rows carry their associations' marks rather than the prescribed ones. North Country does - NCTA's blue map icon. NEW ENGLAND DOES NOT: `net-logo.png` is the NST shield reading 'NEW ENGLAND TRAIL / NATIONAL SCENIC TRAIL', and New England has a 2021-06-28 notice. Corrected 2026-09-30 by review; see `_the_nst_shield_question` above, which is the unresolved part this row must not be read as having settled.) MEASURED 2026-09-30 against the Federal Register API: all 25 'Official Trail Marker' notices were listed, the four trails this file already treats as protected are each on it (Natchez Trace and North Country 2000-03-28, Potomac Heritage 2001-10-25, New England 2021-06-28), and THERE IS NO PACIFIC CREST NOTICE - consistent with those notices being Interior's and the PCT being Agriculture's. Re-run the query rather than trusting this sentence: GET https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json with conditions[term]="official trail marker", order=oldest, and read every title. SCOPE, said plainly: this establishes that the PCT is not on that list. It does NOT establish anything about the other 20 notices or the marks that ship against them. (3) Trademark: PCTA asserts marks in the emblem and this ships as nominative identification of the trail the line actually is, withdrawable at `claim_state` exactly like every other row. Not a grant from this organization and must not be read as one - nor from the Forest Service, whose publication answers copyright and grants nothing else.
